summary:
Canary turns NASA Earth science data into answers anyone can check. Ask “Is soil moisture changing in Kenya?” and Canary gives a plain verdict: rising or falling, by how much per decade, and whether the change is statistically significant or could be chance. It tests 45 years (1981–2025) of NASA POWER data with Mann-Kendall and Theil-Sen trends, corrects for false discoveries, and maps every trend on an interactive 3D globe.

Researchers can dig deeper with: 
- Latitude–time diagrams: a heat map of when and at which latitudes a change appeared.
- Shifting distributions: how often extremes occur, decade by decade.
- A ranking of 26 climate variables for any country or region.

A live mode streams the last 24 hours of NASA GEOS-FP clouds and wind, along with real-time disaster alerts, severe-weather warnings and satellite-detected methane plumes.

This answers the challenge by making trend detection rigorous, transparent and fast. Results come with confidence intervals, downloadable data, citations and API queries. It matters because decisions on drought, heat, water and emissions depend on telling real change from noise, and Canary gives everyone that signal before it becomes a crisis.
details:
What is Canary?

Canary is a trend detective for NASA Earth science data. Pick any of 26 climate variables (air and ground temperature, precipitation, root-zone and surface soil wetness, evaporation, snow, sea ice, cloud, sunlight, humidity, wind, ozone, haze and more) and any of about 200 regions (177 countries, 7 continents, 13 climate regions such as the Arctic, the Sahel or the Amazon basin, or a box you draw on the globe). Canary gives a plain-language verdict: rising or falling, how fast per decade, the likely range, and whether the change is statistically significant or could be chance.

The interface is one interactive 3D globe. It shows where a variable is changing in every grid cell, 1981–2025: bright where the trend is significant, faint where it could be chance. Click a country to investigate it, or click any point for a report on that spot.

How it works

1. Variables: annual grids from NASA POWER, drawn from the MERRA-2 reanalysis and the CERES SYN1deg satellite record and read directly from NASA's public cloud stores. Every variable has a simple definition for non-specialists.

2. Regions: area-weighted averages over country outlines, preset climate regions or drawn boxes, so trends are regional rather than only global.

3. Time series: each year shown as an anomaly from its 1991–2020 normal, the way climate assessments present it.

4. Statistics:

- Theil-Sen slope with a 95% confidence interval.

- Mann-Kendall test, corrected for year-to-year autocorrelation (Hamed-Rao and Yue-Wang).

- Least-squares t-test with an effective sample size.

- Signal-to-noise ratio.

- Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery control whenever thousands of grid cells are tested at once.

If a trend is not yet significant, Canary estimates how many more years of data would settle it, since the challenge notes a trend can be real but too short to confirm.

Beyond a single time series, Canary adds views scientists use:

- A latitude-time (Hovmöller) diagram showing where and when change began.

- Decade-by-decade distributions of local anomalies, showing whether extremes are shifting (after Hansen et al. 2012).

- A forest plot ranking all 26 variables in a region on one scale.

- 3D trend columns on the globe, where only significant change rises.

- "Drivers": correlations with climate modes such as ENSO.

A live mode adds the last 24 hours of NASA GEOS-FP clouds and wind, a geostationary satellite loop from NASA GIBS, and real-time alerts from GDACS, USGS, the US National Weather Service, NASA EONET and Carbon Mapper methane plumes.

Real World Application & Impact

Finding a real trend normally means choosing a dataset, downloading it, subsetting a region, building a time series and running statistics separately. Canary does all of this in seconds, without hiding the method. Every result shows its test, p-value and confidence interval, and can be downloaded as CSV or cited.

Students and the public learn to tell a real signal from noise. Researchers and decision-makers get a fast first look at what is changing where.

Example: the Arctic is warming 0.46 °C per decade, nearly three times the global rate (p < 0.001). The share of Arctic area more than two standard deviations above normal rose from 0.1% in the 1980s to 5.6% since 2020.

Creativity

- Colour carries meaning. Each variable belongs to a family (heat, water, air) that runs between two meaningful ends, and a change only gets colour when it is statistically significant.

- The app shows how one process can push the same variable up in one region and down in another, and includes guided walkthroughs: "The Arctic is warming", "One cause, opposite trends" and "A trend you cannot call yet".

- Maps are rendered as live data on the GPU rather than as static images, so the globe stays smooth at any zoom.

Tools

- Backend: Python (FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, xarray/Zarr).

- Front end: plain JavaScript modules, MapLibre GL JS globe, WebGL2 shaders, SVG charts.

- Testing: Playwright for browser testing, pytest (81 tests).

- Hosting: GitHub Pages.

- Data: NASA POWER (MERRA-2, CERES), NASA GEOS-FP, NASA GIBS, NASA EONET, Carbon Mapper, GDACS, USGS, NOAA NWS.

Factors We Considered

- Statistical honesty. Correcting for autocorrelation and for testing many cells at once matters, because without it most "trends" on a global map are false alarms.

- A beginner audience: plain definitions, guided examples, and confidence stated clearly.

- Accessibility: every status uses a shape as well as a colour, so it works for colour-blind users, and light and dark themes are included.

- Speed: global grids are cached so any region answers instantly.

- Free public access: the live site runs on GitHub Pages with no login.

Live demo site: https://print-eddyma.github.io/Canary/

Code: https://github.com/print-EddyMa/Canary
